lessons.title: WebKit, system authentication, cookies, and bridge lifetimes
lessons.summary: Choose the right browser or authentication API. Check origins, cookie readiness, bridge inputs, and current document ownership before native code acts.
objectives: Tell apart embedded web content, system browsing, web authentication, native requests, and their cookie stores.
Check exact allowed origins and small bridge commands before granting a native action.
Keep authentication and bridge owners alive while rejecting old callbacks and avoiding reference cycles.
Read the current WebKit integration and clearly label system authentication as an alternative where it is not directly implemented.

sections.title: Choose browsing or authentication from the task
sections.html:
Embedded browsing puts web content inside your app’s UI. WKWebView does that. SFSafariViewController provides a system-managed browsing presentation. ASWebAuthenticationSession owns a web sign-in attempt. URLSession sends native requests. Your Android WebView, Custom Tabs, and OkHttp experience helps you ask about these choices, but their cookies and lifetimes differ. Choose from the user’s task and account boundary before adding credentials or native privileges. Sharing a URL does not make the mechanisms interchangeable.

WKWebView coordinates a content process with a native view. A page can navigate, submit forms, open new windows, execute scripts, and crash independently of your controller. A title or trusted starting URL does not make every later navigation trusted. Define whether the feature is displaying first-party content, browsing arbitrary content, or performing authentication before deciding which native privileges it can reach.

The checkout uses WKWebView in its web controller, configures cookies, and applies navigation policies. Searches of active Projects Swift sources did not find a direct ASWebAuthenticationSession call. That is not proof that a dependency never uses it internally. This lesson teaches the system authentication API as an alternative, not a completed replacement for existing login or web flows.

Keep analogies conceptual: iOS cookie stores, presentation anchors, callback delivery, and WebKit process lifetimes are their own APIs. A Compose wrapper around Android WebView does not tell you where a SwiftUI representable should retain a delegate or when an authentication owner should cancel.

sections.title: Make one decision for each navigation request
sections.html:
A navigation delegate receives requests to continue or stop web navigation. Its decision handler is the callback that answers the request. Call it exactly once on every path. Returning without an answer can leave the request unresolved; answering twice violates the callback contract. Define what the feature permits for frames, redirects, schemes, downloads, and external browsing. A nil target frame may request a new window. Then check parsed origins separately from credential eligibility.

Use URLComponents and exact scheme/host/port checks when matching an origin. A hostname ending in a deceptive suffix is not your domain. A path containing “signin” does not necessarily identify the intended endpoint, and percent encoding can affect the interpretation. Navigation permission and credential permission should be separate functions: a page may be viewable while never being eligible for credentials or a JavaScript bridge.

import Foundation

func isSyntheticTrustedOrigin(_ url: URL) -> Bool {
    guard let parts = URLComponents(
        url: url, resolvingAgainstBaseURL: false
    ) else { return false }
    return parts.scheme?.lowercased() == "https"
        && parts.host?.lowercased() == "learn.example.com"
        && parts.user == nil
        && parts.password == nil
        && (parts.port == nil || parts.port == 443)
}

The Boolean expression joins independently named URL properties, not substrings of the complete URL. This Foundation helper only tests origin; it does not prove certificate trust, authorize a resource, or validate a route. TLS uses the system's normal trust evaluation. Never return an unconditional “accept” for an authentication challenge to get around a certificate failure.

The active controller has first-party/external flags and specific legacy path/scheme actions. Read them as observed product policy. They are not a reusable complete trust policy for arbitrary web browsing or every authentication flow.

sections.title: Wait for cookies and recheck the current account
sections.html:
A cookie store owns web session data. WKWebsiteDataStore supplies WebKit’s data store, and WKHTTPCookieStore exposes its cookie operations. URLSession and HTTPCookieStorage are separate boundaries. Updating one does not instantly update every other store. Persistent and non-persistent WebKit stores also have different retention rules. After asynchronous setup, recheck which account and document still own the load. Non-persistence is not permission to copy credentials into JavaScript or to skip logout cleanup.

Cookies have domain, path, secure, expiry, and other attributes that constrain use. Native header authentication is different from page cookie authentication. A header added to an initial URLRequest is not a guarantee that every later web navigation, subresource, or redirect carries it correctly. Conversely, a broadly scoped cookie can reach requests beyond the single initial page. Follow the service's intended session contract.

The active WebViewController sets cookies through completion callbacks and resolves them before loading its request. It also adds a bearer header only under current login, trusted-domain, and HTTPS checks. That is a concrete readiness and credential boundary. It does not prove arbitrary redirects preserve the same checks or that cookie teardown reaches every WebKit store.

Logout ends more than a visible page. Native account state, Keychain data, HTTP cookies, WebKit website data, pending work, and visible content have separate cleanup paths. The inspected account code deletes selected HTTPCookieStorage cookies. Trace the chosen WebKit store before claiming its data is cleared too. Also guard setup completions: if A’s cookies finish after logout or B’s login, the old epoch must prevent starting an A-authenticated page. A current view controller alone is not current account ownership.

sections.title: Give web messages only a small native action
sections.html:
A bridge lets web-controlled input request native behavior. That is a capability: permission to ask for a particular action. Define a small command set with bounded payloads, versioning if needed, frame and origin rules, and explicit outcomes. A close command should not grow into arbitrary native method calls, file access, or authenticated URL loading. Even a trusted site can be compromised. Minimize the granted action and keep service authorization separate from the message’s accepted shape.

This WebKit example requires a platform target. The user-content controller can retain the receiver, while the receiver weakly references the UI owner. It accepts one harmless synthetic command and no extra fields:

import WebKit

@MainActor
protocol CourseWebOwner: AnyObject {
    func closeRequested()
}

@MainActor
final class CourseBridge: NSObject, WKScriptMessageHandler {
    weak var owner: (any CourseWebOwner)?

    func userContentController(
        _ userContentController: WKUserContentController,
        didReceive message: WKScriptMessage
    ) {
        let origin = message.frameInfo.securityOrigin
        guard message.name == "courseBridge",
              message.frameInfo.isMainFrame,
              origin.protocol == "https",
              origin.host.lowercased() == "learn.example.com",
              origin.port == 0 || origin.port == 443,
              let body = message.body as? [String: String],
              body.count == 1,
              body["command"] == "close" else { return }
        owner?.closeRequested()
    }
}

AnyObject restricts the owner protocol to reference types, enabling weak storage. any expresses a protocol existential. Optional chaining safely handles a disappeared owner. MainActor matches current WebKit's handler isolation. Install with the agreed name, and remove the handler at the feature's stopping event. A weak owner avoids one cycle but does not automatically unregister a stale bridge.

Content worlds can help separate script namespaces on supported APIs, but are not a service-authorization boundary. Handle page replacement and disabled features so an old document cannot continue issuing valid-looking commands.

sections.title: Keep results tied to the current document
sections.html:
A document generation is a changing identifier for the page that owns current work. JavaScript evaluation can finish after navigation has replaced that page. evaluateJavaScript also interprets script source: interpolating user text can break syntax or inject code. Prefer argument-passing APIs such as callAsyncJavaScript where supported, then validate the returned types, size, and shape. These APIs do not replace ownership checks. The current document, scene, account, and feature must still want the result before native code applies it.

Capture a document generation before asynchronous script evaluation. After it finishes, confirm the same document, scene, account, and feature still own the result. Navigating to a new page can leave an old completion pending. A controller remaining alive does not prove that completion belongs to the current document. Cancellation helps reduce work but may not retract a previously submitted JavaScript operation.

Retain required delegate/coordinator owners when bridging UIKit into SwiftUI, and explicitly stop loading and unregister messages during teardown. Be careful with closure captures: owner to web view to user-content controller to handler to owner can form a cycle. A weak forwarding owner plus removal breaks the obvious retention path; inspect other stored callbacks too. Weak capture solves retention, not authorization or stale commits.

Implement content-process termination and navigation failures with a bounded recovery policy. A page reload may be safe for a read-only page and unsafe for a submitted form whose server effect is uncertain. Do not treat every web error as permission to replay a side effect. Session 018's idempotency reasoning also applies here.

sections.title: Give each sign-in attempt an owner
sections.html:
An authentication session owns one system-managed web sign-in attempt and its callback. ASWebAuthenticationSession is available from iOS 12, while individual initializers, callback matching, and presentation APIs have later requirements. Current documentation includes newer callback APIs and deprecates an older scheme initializer. Check each symbol against the selected SDK and deployment range before using it in an iOS 17 target. Retaining the session, presenting in the right scene, and validating the protocol remain separate responsibilities.

A coordinator retains the session and presentation-context provider, uses an anchor from the correct active scene, and handles the Boolean result of start. Failing to start is different from the person canceling. Provide a meaningful recovery state without a prompt loop. Cancel when the owning attempt ends, clear retained state on terminal completion, and reject callbacks from superseded attempts.

Protocol validation checks that a callback belongs to the login attempt you started. For OAuth or OpenID Connect, check the exact callback destination and state bound to that attempt. Use PKCE where required to tie code exchange to its starter. Use nonce for the appropriate identity-token flow. Browser isolation does not replace these checks or service authorization. Keep callback URLs, codes, tokens, and full identity claims out of logs. Then let the current account owner accept the validated result.

An ephemeral preference requests an appropriate private authentication session; it is not a guarantee that every identity provider forgets server-side login or that your existing WKWebView shares the same cookies. Credentials stay with the established networking/account owner after exchange. A successful browser callback alone should not install account data until that owner validates the current attempt.

sections.title: Check trust, lifetime, and real browser behavior separately
sections.html:
A trust boundary is the point where input gains permission to affect another part of the app. Read the cookie completion chain, trusted HTTPS header check, navigation decisions, and native cookie cleanup together. State what each proves and what remains unknown. A source path check describes the current product flow. It does not establish that the teaching bridge is installed or that logout clears the selected WebKit store. Those claims need their own source trace and platform observations.

Use synthetic fixtures for deceptive hosts, unknown schemes, malformed messages, wrong frame origins, additional fields, new-window actions, redirected navigation, and a document change before script completion. For identity, pause cookie setup, log out, then release it; no old page should load. Pause authentication, start another attempt, then return the first callback; it must not replace the new attempt's state.

A fake completion chain can verify ordering but cannot prove actual cookie propagation, browser sharing, identity-provider compatibility, TLS challenges, or content-process failure recovery. Those need platform targets and, where applicable, signed devices and a controlled test service. UI screenshots show visible states, not absence of stale credentials.

Keep residual specialist work explicit: enterprise SSO, passkeys, advanced browser policies, certificate operations, complex document downloads, and third-party authentication SDK internals need deeper review. No production credentials, login sessions, cookies, or website data are read or modified by this lesson.

To make the cookie-readiness schedule observable, record load requests in a fake array. Begin ticket A, hold setup, invalidate on logout, then release setup and assert the array remains empty. Begin ticket B and finish setup while current; assert exactly one load for B. Replaying A’s completion must not add a load. Repeat the stale-failure schedule and assert it cannot replace B’s visible state. These tests exercise the ownership seam; they do not prove cookie deletion, redirect credentials, WebKit process recovery, or system authentication behavior.

quiz.question: Cookies were written to HTTPCookieStorage.shared. What does that prove about WKWebView?
options: Every WebKit data store is already updated.

quiz.explanation: Native networking and WebKit have distinct stores and asynchronous operations. Verify the selected store and await readiness before loading.

quiz.question: A bridge uses a weak owner. Is the trust boundary complete?
options: Yes, weak references validate website identity.
No; still validate origin/frame/message and unregister stale handlers.

quiz.explanation: Weak ownership prevents a retention path. It does not authorize a message, constrain payloads, or stop an old document using an installed bridge.

quiz.question: A system authentication callback arrives after a second login attempt started. What should happen?
options: Always install its token because the system returned it.
Validate attempt ownership and protocol fields before any credential commit.
Reload the current WKWebView to fix state.
quiz.explanation: The callback can be valid for an obsolete attempt. Current generation, exact redirect, state, and the flow's protections must be checked before installing credentials.

exercise.brief: Design a synthetic web boundary with an exact-origin check, one bridge command, a fake cookie-readiness gate, and an authentication-attempt record. Keep real identity providers closed.
steps: Test the origin rule with trusted HTTPS, a deceptive host, HTTP, embedded credentials, and an unexpected port.
Define CourseBridge’s allowed message and frame. Extract a pure decision function to test those limits.
Hold fake cookie setup, invalidate account ownership, then release the setup and check that no old page loads.
Give document changes and login attempts separate generations. Reject completions from old generations.

acceptance: Origin matching uses parsed properties rather than URL substrings.

exercise.solution:
The worked rule grants credential eligibility only to the synthetic HTTPS origin. The bridge accepts one main-frame close command. Origin matching does not parse a route or prove TLS trust. Give each document a changing generation, and remove the named handler when the native action is no longer offered. For cookie readiness, use the MainActor gate below. It models current ownership without creating a web view, setting real cookies, or opening an authentication provider.

Use this MainActor value to model the readiness decision without a web view or real cookies:

@MainActor
final class WebAttemptGate {
    private var generation = 0

    func begin() -> Int {
        generation += 1
        return generation
    }

    func invalidate() { generation += 1 }

    func isCurrent(_ ticket: Int) -> Bool {
        ticket == generation
    }
}

Capture begin's ticket before cookie work. After awaiting the fake, check cancellation, account/document ownership, and isCurrent before starting a load. No await should separate the final decision from the load call on MainActor. Authentication has a separate attempt owner with terminal state; a valid redirect for attempt one must still fail ownership after attempt two begins.

The fixture matrix accepts a trusted origin and one close body, rejects deceptive host and extra fields, rejects a subframe, and ignores callbacks after invalidation. For retention review, draw owner to web view to configuration/content controller to handler, then identify the weak edge and explicit removal. Add page termination and teardown to the pending platform matrix.

The checkout review states that cookies are awaited before load and initial bearer attachment has login/domain/HTTPS predicates, while native logout deletes selected HTTP cookies. It asks for evidence covering the selected WebKit data store and redirects rather than claiming a leak. No SDK internals or identity-provider runtime flow were verified by this worked answer.

simple.story: Tara prepares a visitor badge for Alex. The badge is ready only after the front desk finishes checking it. Before that happens, Alex’s visit is canceled and Bea arrives. lessons.title: Device capability, permission states, location, maps, photos, and camera
lessons.summary: Treat permission, hardware, service health, and flow ownership as separate questions. Offer useful fallbacks for location, selected photos, maps, and still capture.
objectives: Check OS support, hardware, permission, service state, and account eligibility separately.
Define useful behavior for denied, restricted, limited, approximate, unavailable, and canceled cases.
Trace the current location, map, photo-picker, and camera implementations.
Own camera operations and callbacks so stopping a flow prevents late results from restarting it.

sections.title: Ask more than whether permission is granted
sections.html:
A capability is the ability to perform an operation under the current conditions. Permission is one condition. As on Android, granted camera permission does not create a camera, and granted location permission does not produce a GPS fix. Check five separate questions: OS support, hardware support, authorization, service usability, and account eligibility. They can change independently. An import or usage-description string answers only part of the contract. Preserve the framework’s states instead of reducing them all to one Boolean.

Frameworks use different authorization states. Camera has not-determined, authorized, denied, and restricted. Photos can grant limited library access. Location adds when-in-use versus always and an accuracy authorization dimension. Notifications have still other statuses and presentation settings. Do not build one global “PermissionStatus” enum that erases distinctions consumers need. Normalize only at a well-defined feature boundary.

Denied generally means the person declined access; repeated requests usually do not show the original prompt again. Restricted can represent parental or managed-device policy that the person cannot simply change in app Settings. Not-determined means a contextual request may be possible, not that it must occur during startup. Authorized means permitted scope, not successful operation. Unknown future states need a conservative, useful fallback.

Usage descriptions explain why the app requests access and are required for relevant protected APIs. A capability entitlement can grant a different kind of system access. Neither is the runtime decision. Session 026 covers signed artifacts; verify the descriptions and capabilities in the actual target, including extensions, rather than assuming the main app's plist covers every process.

sections.title: Separate location permission from a usable fix
sections.html:
A location fix is a reported position with time and accuracy information. It is different from authorization to ask for one. CLLocationManager owns a delegate-driven service and needs a retained owner with the required run-loop and isolation behavior. Request when-in-use access when the task needs it, after checking status. Always access and background location are separate feature decisions. They are not routine upgrades for keeping a search page alive. Approximate scope, disabled services, and stale fixes need separate outcomes.

On supported OS versions, full versus reduced accuracy is a separate authorization value. Accept an approximate location when it meets the search contract; temporary precision requests require a specific user benefit and appropriate purpose configuration. Do not interpret reduced accuracy as denial. A CLLocation also includes timestamp and accuracy metadata. A stale fix or invalid horizontal accuracy should not become “current precise location” just because a callback returned a coordinate.

Use one-shot requests when the task only needs one fix, and stop ongoing updates at the owner's stopping event. Handle service-disabled, denied, restricted, temporarily unavailable, and timeout/cancellation outcomes independently. A permitted request can still fail indoors or on a simulator with no location set. Offer manual location selection rather than routing every failure to Settings.

The active LocationPermissionService separates authorization prompting from GPS fetch, checks global services, and offers manual/Settings recovery. Its code notes that a fetch can fail despite permission. Read the continuations and foreground observer lifetime as well: a screen disappearing while waiting must have a defined stop outcome, and a checked continuation alone does not implement cancellation.

sections.title: Keep manual map browsing usable without GPS
sections.html:
MapKit displays maps, regions, and annotations. It can show known provider coordinates without requesting the person’s location. A current-location indicator or a location-dependent action needs the relevant authorization and service checks. Keep these tasks separate. Denying GPS should still allow a map of a manually selected city when the product supports that task. Your Android map experience transfers the distinction, while MapKit’s region, annotation, and delegate APIs still need their own learning and tests.

The checkout uses an MKMapView inside a MapViewController, maintains provider locations and search identities, and has dedicated map delegate code. A source map view proves an implemented rendering path, not successful geocoding, routing, or position tracking on every device. Region changes can trigger search; avoid feedback loops where applying results changes region and launches another identical request.

Coordinate order matters: latitude and longitude are distinct fields, measured in degrees. Validate finite values and allowed ranges before creating domain input. Zero-zero can be a legitimate coordinate, so it should not automatically mean “missing.” A map projection's screen distance is not simply degree subtraction. Use appropriate geospatial APIs and service contracts for distance, route duration, and region bounds.

Geocoding and directions are asynchronous services that can fail or be constrained. Cancel obsolete requests, guard their generation after waiting, and keep manual addresses usable. Opening Maps through a map item transfers a task to another app; it does not give your process indefinite navigation background execution. Full navigation, offline maps, advanced geospatial search, and location privacy need separate specialist practice.

sections.title: Use selected-photo access when that is enough
sections.html:
A system photo picker lets the person choose particular assets for the app. It often meets an upload task without broad PhotoKit library authorization. PHPickerViewController is available from iOS 14 and SwiftUI PhotosPicker from iOS 16. A selected item offers asynchronous access to the chosen asset. It is not already a UIImage, an unrestricted file path, or a grant to browse the whole library. Handle loading, cancellation, newer selections, and limited-library access as different situations.

PhotoKit's read/write and add-only access scopes have different purposes. Limited access allows only selected assets and is useful authorization, not an error to “fix” by forcing full access. Asset visibility can change after the person edits their limited selection. A cached asset identifier may no longer resolve. Check status for the intended access level and provide a scoped recovery path instead of assuming one Boolean grants every operation.

Selected data may wait for an iCloud download, format conversion, or decoding. The person can cancel or choose another photo before it finishes. Retain the work handle, request cancellation for old work, and check a selection generation before updating the preview. Cancellation alone cannot promise that the old result never returns. Large image decoding also needs a measured memory budget and appropriate downsampling. Lesson 039 develops that work. Requesting JPEG does not by itself bound peak memory use.

The active card-capture view model stores a PhotosPickerItem. That establishes current picker integration, while broader library editing and asset management remain separate. Review export orientation, metadata retention, temporary-file deletion, upload authorization, and account ownership. A selected image can contain sensitive identity or location metadata; use synthetic images for this course.

sections.title: Own session setup, capture, and stopping
sections.html:
A capture session connects camera inputs and outputs. AVCaptureSession owns that connection. A device input represents the available capture device; AVCapturePhotoOutput returns still-photo results through delegate callbacks. The preview and captured data serve different consumers. Authorized hardware may still be absent, interrupted, busy, or unable to provide the format you want. Give configuration, start, stop, and recovery one serialized owner. Moving work off the UI thread alone does not make these operations ordered.

Session configuration must happen in a consistent order. Use beginConfiguration and commitConfiguration, check whether each input and output can be added, and preserve setup errors. Starting and stopping may block, so keep expensive startup off the UI thread. Give configuration, start, stop, and interruption recovery one serialized owner. Sending independent calls to a global concurrent queue keeps them away from the UI but does not order them. Test rapid stop and restart as well as ordinary capture.

The checked CameraSessionManager is MainActor-facing, uses background global queues for start/stop, retains its photo delegate, and has a simulator placeholder path. Those are actual source choices. They do not prove every start/stop race is resolved or that simulator permission success validates hardware capture. A review should test serialized lifecycle ownership and interruption cases before endorsing a reusable camera architecture.

Rotation and mirroring affect both preview and output. Current AVFoundation offers availability-qualified rotation APIs such as videoRotationAngle; the source still uses an older videoOrientation path. Inspect supported OS and connection capabilities before updating it. Still capture fundamentals are covered here; real-time video, audio routing, synchronization, DSP, codecs, and telehealth performance remain specialist branches.

sections.title: Decide the action before showing a system prompt
sections.html:
A pure policy function chooses an outcome without performing the system action. This lets a test distinguish request authorization, offer manual input, and start capture. The function below deliberately models one synthetic camera feature. It is not a universal permission service. Hardware presence and the four camera grant states are separate inputs. Decide first, then let an adapter request access or start capture. After any wait, check the current status and whether the flow still owns the result.

enum CameraGrant: Sendable {
    case neverAsked, authorized, denied, restricted
}
enum CameraPlan: Equatable, Sendable {
    case request
    case capture
    case manualNoDevice
    case manualDenied
    case manualRestricted
}

func cameraPlan(
    grant: CameraGrant,
    hasDevice: Bool
) -> CameraPlan {
    guard hasDevice else { return .manualNoDevice }
    switch grant {
    case .neverAsked: return .request
    case .authorized: return .capture
    case .denied: return .manualDenied
    case .restricted: return .manualRestricted
    }
}

The enums make outcomes explicit. The first guard avoids prompting for unavailable hardware. The exhaustive switch ensures known states have defined behavior. An adapter maps AVAuthorizationStatus, including unknown future values conservatively, then a UI owner interprets the plan. Requesting access is an effect executed after the decision, not inside this pure function.

After the request returns, re-read current status and feature ownership. The user may have dismissed the screen or the account may have changed. A positive Boolean from the authorization callback must not automatically start a stopped flow. Keep an owner generation around that await. A one-shot capture callback also needs exactly-once delivery and a policy for late data.

For callbacks wrapped in continuations, serialize completion versus cancellation, resume once, and stop the underlying operation where supported. A checked continuation detects certain misuse; it does not invent cancellation or prevent an indefinitely retained observer. Do not use an unsynchronized Boolean as the entire race solution.

sections.title: Give each state a useful fallback
sections.html:
A fallback is another way the person can complete the task when the preferred operation is unavailable. Denied camera can offer a photo picker or manual entry. Restricted camera should not promise that Settings can remove a policy. Approximate location may support a wider nearby search; failed GPS can keep a manually selected city. Limited photos remain useful for accessible selected assets. Check keyboard access, Dynamic Type, and VoiceOver for each fallback, then record the device states still needing observation.

Re-query relevant state on returning from Settings, but do not assume a change occurred. Retain and remove foreground observers according to the flow's lifetime. The checkout's location service awaits foreground then fetches; a canceled owner, failed Settings opening, or another scene transition deserves an explicit verification case. Global application notifications can be insufficient to identify which scene owns the result.

A physical-device matrix includes first request, denial, restriction where available, Settings change, approximate location, disabled services, missing or interrupted hardware, picker cancellation, iCloud-loading failure, and rapid start-stop. Simulator fixtures are valuable for deterministic policy and UI checks. The source's placeholder image deliberately bypasses hardware, so record it as simulation rather than actual capture evidence.

Bluetooth, motion/sensors, HealthKit and regulatory policy, ML-based recognition, and other specialized device services are further study. This lesson provides transferable ownership questions but does not implement those services or certify clinical camera/location workflows. Use current official docs and target-specific evidence before expanding scope.

exercise.brief: Test the camera decision and a fake flow-ownership gate. Make a fallback table for location, photo selection, and still capture without requesting real permission.
steps: Check all four CameraGrant cases with hardware present and absent.
Hold fake authorization, stop the flow, then return granted and verify that capture cannot start.
Hold two fake photo selections. Finish the newer one first and the older one last.
Give denied, restricted, approximate, unavailable, and manual-location cases separate rows.
Read camera session and location observer sources, then list pending physical-device checks.
acceptance: Missing hardware never triggers a permission request.
Denied and restricted states have distinct explanations and workable fallbacks.
Late authorization never starts a stopped camera flow.
Only the current photo selection replaces the preview.
Simulator placeholder behavior is reported separately from device capture and permission verification.
exercise.solution:
The camera rule has eight combinations: four grant states, each with hasDevice false and true. Every false row returns manualNoDevice. The true rows return request, capture, manualDenied, or manualRestricted for the corresponding grant. Keep this camera-specific model separate from Photos and Location states. The flow gate below models the owner around a wait. It lets a test stop the flow before an authorization response and check that even a granted late response cannot restart it.

@MainActor
final class DeviceFlowGate {
    private var generation = 0
    private var active = false

    func start() -> Int {
        generation += 1
        active = true
        return generation
    }

    func stop() {
        active = false
        generation += 1
    }

    func accepts(_ ticket: Int) -> Bool {
        active && ticket == generation
    }
}

Capture start's ticket before a fake authorization await. Stop the flow before releasing the fake; accepts must be false even if access is granted. For photo selection, start a new generation for each chosen item and release the older transfer last. Only the current ticket can replace the preview. In a real feature, combine this guard with retained task cancellation and a serialized capture-session owner.

The location matrix has independent columns for authorization, accuracy, global services, fix freshness, and owner lifetime. A manual city keeps map browsing available. The device ledger requests prompt outcomes, Settings-return behavior, restricted-state messaging, session interruption/start-stop ordering, preview/output rotation, and a large or remotely stored selected image. It marks those observations pending until executed.

The source review notes that global background dispatch avoids UI blocking but does not by itself serialize session operations. It also notes retained photo delegates and simulator bypass. This is a bounded design and synthetic test plan, not a camera migration or a proof that every existing callback race is safe.

lessons.title: Extensions, widgets, App Intents, and platform integration review
lessons.summary: Follow one feature across app, widget, and intent boundaries. Keep shared data, account ownership, repeated commands, and system refresh promises explicit.
objectives: Tell apart the app process, extension, shared code, App Group storage, and system-rendered content.
Plan widget timelines and intent actions without promising exact refresh times.
Check current ownership and stable command identity at the shared write boundary.
Write an integration record showing what was explained, tested, and left for specialist or device work.

sections.title: Shared code does not share a running app
sections.html:
A process has its own live memory and execution owners. An app extension is a separately built executable with its own bundle ID, entry setup, and constrained lifetime. Android services and widgets suggest useful questions, but importing a shared Swift module does not share the app’s heap, dependency container, window, or session singleton. It shares code. The containing app can embed an extension without staying alive to serve it. App Group storage adds a different, explicit sharing boundary.

The system or a host invokes the extension under an extension-specific contract. A notification service extension modifies eligible remote notifications; a WidgetKit extension supplies timeline content. A share extension handles a host request with its own completion and cancellation semantics. These are different mechanisms, not interchangeable places to run arbitrary background work. Some application APIs are unavailable to extensions, so compile shared code with the appropriate extension-safe settings and check imports.

App Groups grant entitled targets access to a named shared container. They do not provide a shared actor, transaction queue, automatic account synchronization, or unrestricted access to another app. Keychain sharing uses separate access-group controls. Inspect signed entitlements and actual container resolution in each target. A matching literal in source is necessary evidence but does not prove provisioning or runtime container access.

The active app manifest embeds App Clip, Notifications, and MedicationWidget targets. The notification extension subclasses Braze's service, and the medication core module is reused from the widget. This is implemented source support. Specialized share, keyboard, file-provider, network, and credential-provider extensions remain further study rather than implied support.

sections.title: Check each extension’s dependencies and resources
sections.html:
Packaging puts a target’s executable, metadata, and resources into its delivered product. An extension needs its own Info.plist extension point, OS support, resources, entitlements, and dependency graph. A shared library can be unsuitable if it reaches UIApplication or app-only navigation, even when one helper inside it is useful. Read public APIs with target dependencies. A small extension-safe core can keep domain rules separate from app presentation and analytics. Its resource bundle still needs the correct owner and lookup.

The checkout's medication package has a core target with no package dependencies, while its app-facing target depends on UI and module infrastructure. The core still imports Apple frameworks in particular files; zero package dependencies is not a claim of universal platform independence. Its host-tooling guards and iOS availability need inspection per file. The app manifest declares MedicationWidget as an app extension with an iOS 17 floor.

Resource ownership matters here just as in session 022: an extension's bundle and a package's resource bundle are distinct. A localization key in the containing app is not automatically visible to its extension. A widget preview must use suitable synthetic placeholders, not load a person's current data merely to show a gallery example.

Validate embedding and extension-safe linking in the final archive, not only in package unit tests. Keep artifact identities for the app and embedded products. Source manifests establish packaging intent; a signed install and actual extension invocation establish runtime integration. No archive or device build was performed for this course-content edit.

sections.title: Hand the system a content plan for the widget
sections.html:
A widget timeline is a plan of content entries associated with dates. TimelineEntry describes one entry; TimelineProvider supplies placeholders, snapshots, and the plan. Gallery and placeholder paths should be cheap and synthetic. The system can render planned changes without keeping the extension running. Think of handing over a schedule of content rather than owning a permanently active screen. Reload policies request opportunities for new entries. They cannot promise an exact refresh time or instant removal of a cached snapshot.

Reload policies such as atEnd or after request a later opportunity for a new timeline. WidgetCenter reload requests tell the system that existing content is obsolete. Neither is an exact scheduling contract. Dynamic resource budgets and visibility affect updates. A counter or deadline must use appropriate system-supported time rendering or a stale-state design; do not create a per-second timer and assume the extension remains alive.

The active MedicationWidgetTimelineProvider returns empty placeholder/gallery content, reads the shared store for actual snapshots, builds entries, and uses atEnd. Its pure WidgetTimelineBuilder is a useful test seam. The source's predicted entries and refresh request do not establish that every device renders each transition at an exact instant or that an unavailable protected file becomes readable.

Privacy includes cached snapshots and system surfaces. Sensitive details can remain in a rendered timeline after the source changes until the system processes a reload. Request reload after logout and minimize what the widget displays by design. Treat actual stale-snapshot visibility and locked-screen behavior as device verification, not something proved by deleting the backing file.

sections.title: An intent declares an action and still needs checks
sections.html:
An AppIntent declares an operation, its metadata, parameters, and async perform method for system invocation. @Parameter is a property wrapper used in that representation. Its title is visible metadata, not a normal Codable storage key. some IntentResult names an opaque result type that conforms to the required interface. It does not mean any arbitrary object. Availability, execution location, current account, and durable success still need explicit rules. MainActor identifies the selected process’s isolation domain, not another app process.

An intent can open the app and route into UI, or act from a widget or another system surface. Its configuration and system behavior determine where it executes. MainActor isolates UI-related state within that selected process. It is not one actor shared by the app and every extension, and it is not a dedicated thread for this intent. Shared intent code therefore cannot assume app-only singleton instances exist just because perform uses MainActor. Declare the real process and dependency owner.

The checkout's BookAgainIntent sets openAppWhenRun and routes through an injected IntentRouter. The router buffers one destination until UI wiring exists. Its isDiscoverable setting is false, so do not describe the type as automatically publishing every action to broad shortcut discovery. Trace explicit donation and registration paths when making discovery claims.

The widget's MarkDoseTakenIntent passes an occurrence identity to shared mutation logic and then requests reload. That identity guards against recomputing “today” from a stale entry. Its source suppresses some store failures, which means returning a result is not proof a write succeeded. A production success contract needs explicit durable evidence and an intentional user-facing failure policy.

sections.title: Whole-file replacement does not combine two edits
sections.html:
A read-modify-write operation loads old data, changes it, and saves the replacement. Atomic replacement prevents readers seeing a partial file. It does not stop two processes loading the same old data and later overwriting each other’s changes. An actor in the app and one in an extension are separate owners. Their MainActors are separate too. Real multi-writer storage needs a transactional store, coordinated command protocol, or another reviewed interprocess mechanism. Shared access alone cannot supply that rule.

The inspected widget intent loads a reminder collection, transforms it, saves it, and reloads. The file store atomically replaces JSON. These sources do not establish an interprocess read-modify-write lock. This is a conditional concurrency risk requiring targeted verification, not a claim that a lost update was reproduced. Similarly, try? save followed by reload can leave visible content unchanged without exposing the save error to the caller.

An operation ID prevents replay only while the mutation rule can still remember it. Account ownership decides which session may apply it. Persist both in the relevant transaction when effects must survive restart. A process-local Set is not durable replay protection. An account string cannot distinguish an old A login from a later A login after B. If logout clears shared records, reject stale widget commands before they can recreate them. Validate ownership where the write actually occurs.

The shared location helper centralizes container path and retention and offers app-local fallback when the group is unavailable. That fallback can keep app UI working while the widget cannot see those local records. Diagnose the missing shared capability separately from “the reminders disappeared.” Migration into the group is also an app-owned operation, not a widget entitlement workaround.

sections.title: Practice repeated and old-owner commands
sections.html:
A command is a checked request for one operation. Here it acknowledges a harmless synthetic card and carries an owner epoch, operation ID, and card ID. The operation ID distinguishes replay; the epoch rejects an old owner. The actor below models only one process’s memory. It has no file, App Group, or server. An actor isolates access to its state rather than assigning a dedicated thread. Use the example to check ordering and outcomes, then state what durability remains absent.

struct SurfaceCommand: Sendable {
    let ownerEpoch: Int
    let operationID: String
    let cardID: String
}
enum SurfaceOutcome: Equatable, Sendable {
    case applied, duplicate, stale, unknownCard
}

actor SyntheticSurfaceStore {
    private var epoch = 1
    private var cards: Set<String> = ["alpha", "beta"]
    private var applied: Set<String> = []
    private var acknowledged: Set<String> = []

    func currentEpoch() -> Int { epoch }

    func resetOwner() {
        epoch += 1
        cards = []
        applied = []
        acknowledged = []
    }

    func apply(_ command: SurfaceCommand) -> SurfaceOutcome {
        guard command.ownerEpoch == epoch else { return .stale }
        guard cards.contains(command.cardID) else { return .unknownCard }
        guard !applied.contains(command.operationID) else {
            return .duplicate
        }
        acknowledged.insert(command.cardID)
        applied.insert(command.operationID)
        return .applied
    }

    func values() -> Set<String> { acknowledged }
}

The command is immutable and Sendable. Set membership gives an explicit replay policy. apply has no suspension between validation and mutation, so resetOwner cannot interleave inside that actor transition. A caller uses await to enter the actor. The code rejects unknown cards and old epochs rather than recreating absent data. A network-facing version must also bound and validate command fields.

This is a memory fake, not an App Group store or a server. Restarting it loses deduplication history. Two processes would each have their own instance. A durable implementation must make account validation, mutation, and operation recording part of one actual transaction and define how history expires.

sections.title: Name the specialist work still outside this checkout
sections.html:
Platform support means more than reusing a Swift type. watchOS needs its own targets, lifecycle, connectivity, background budgets, and complications. visionOS adds scene, input, and spatial design work. CloudKit synchronization adds account identity, versions, conflicts, offline queues, and schema deployment. The inspected app manifest declares neither watchOS nor visionOS products. This unit implements none of these branches. The table names further practice so an API mention cannot be mistaken for completed feature support.

These are explicit further-study boundaries, not hidden lessons claimed complete by an API mention. The course teaches still-capture permission and ownership basics, not a real-time media pipeline; timeline reasoning, not a production watch complication; migration fundamentals, not a replicated database. If an actual feature requires one of these branches, create a scoped specialist learning and validation plan.

Current Apple documentation can expose capabilities newer than the checkout's deployment floor. Record API availability separately from target minimum, toolchain pins, enabled capabilities, and runtime verification. A library present in a lockfile likewise does not prove the product implements its full platform feature set.

sections.title: Review one card flow across all seven lessons
sections.html:
An integration review checks how boundaries work together in one flow. Use a synthetic card opened from a link. It needs login, reads a cache, may choose an image, and shows a widget acknowledgment. Lesson 050 handles execution and notification outcomes. Lesson 051 parses and gates the route. Lesson 052 defines time, text, and file meaning. Lesson 053 owns persistent snapshots. Lesson 054 owns web or sign-in boundaries. Lesson 055 owns device effects. This lesson adds extension commands.

For each boundary write input, trust level, owner, isolation or process, durable effect, terminal outcome, and acceptance evidence. Control ordering with gates: logout before a delayed response, second route before login finishes, new document before script callback, stopped camera before permission returns, duplicate widget action, and shared-store failure before reload. The same case can cross several layers; do not declare success because each individual helper passes its happy path.

Separate source observations, executed synthetic checks, planned target/device checks, and specialist branches in the handoff. Verify active source paths and line anchors, not an obsolete duplicate file. No unit exercise authorizes editing app source, changing live accounts, publishing an extension, or pre-completing learner progress. Use standalone scratch work and synthetic data.

A useful integration review ends with precise residual risks: actual shared-store serialization, signed App Group access, archived extension resources, widget snapshot privacy, real notification and universal-link delivery, locked-device failures, and authentication/device-service behavior. This is a substantial foundation for platform work, not a claim to exhaust all of iOS.

The worked review separates staff ownership of one shared command seam from principal ownership of its adoption across teams. The staff-principal-decisions workshop supplies options, cost assumptions, accountable owners, adoption gates, future-operation rollback, and old-path deprecation criteria. Its synthetic strategy is a review exercise. A single-process actor fixture and a polished RFC cannot establish cross-process durability, installed-client compatibility, or organizational adoption.

A reload was requested; privacy design and observed system refresh still need verification.

Only if the operation ID is a UUID.
quiz.explanation: Sendable concerns safe transfer, not disk durability. Separate processes or restarts do not share this actor's in-memory Set.

exercise.brief: Check the synthetic surface-command actor and review one complete card flow. Read widget, intent, and App Group code without changing the client or learner progress.
steps: Apply the same command twice. Check applied, then duplicate, with one acknowledgment.
Hold a command, reset ownership, then release it. Check stale and confirm that cleared data stays absent.
Add design rows for an unknown card and a failed durable write.
Follow target embedding, the shared store path, placeholder content, and intent routing.
Create a seven-lesson evidence table that separates explained behavior, executed fakes, pending platform checks, and specialist work.
acceptance: Repeated commands cannot duplicate the synthetic effect.
Old ownership cannot resurrect cleared records.
The actor is labeled memory-only and single-process.
Widget reload is not described as an exact scheduling or instant privacy guarantee.
Repository support is distinguished from unimplemented specialist platforms.
The final ledger includes all seven sessions with measurable boundary outcomes.
exercise.solution:
Start with the actor’s current epoch and create command r1 for card alpha. The first apply returns applied; the second returns duplicate. values contains alpha once. Hold another command, call resetOwner, then release it. It returns stale and the acknowledged set stays empty. A command for an unknown card at the current epoch returns unknownCard without changing state. These are memory-only predictions until you execute the fixture. They do not prove a shared file transaction or a real widget update.

The integration ledger makes ownership and evidence reviewable:

BoundaryAcceptanceEvidence still needed
Background/notificationOne completion; expired or old-account work cannot commitSigned-device APNs and execution observations
Route/loginBounded parser; only current pending route navigatesAASA, installed identity, cold/warm taps, App Clip invocation
Foundation/storageNamed civil-time policy; correct ranges; preserved failuresLocked-file attributes, upgrade fixtures, backup behavior
Web/device servicesNo stale cookie, document, permission, or selection commitControlled provider, WebKit, hardware and Settings behavior
Widget/intentStable command identity; no stale record resurrectionInterprocess transaction, signed App Group, cached snapshot review

A durable command design records operation identity and effect atomically under current account ownership. The process that renders a timeline reads an immutable projection, not an app-owned managed object. If the write fails, define a bounded visible failure outcome and do not report durable success merely because perform returned a result. Request reload after successful state changes and cleanup, while acknowledging system-controlled rendering.

The source review records active MedicationWidget embedding, the placeholder/snapshot distinction, the group path helper and its fallback, BookAgain's app-opening route, and MarkDoseTaken's shared mutation path. It calls out read-modify-write coordination and suppressed write errors as questions needing verification, not reproduced incidents. The specialist ledger names media/DSP, Metal, Bluetooth, HealthKit/regulatory, StoreKit, watchOS/visionOS, CloudKit, ML, specialized extensions, and unsafe APIs as further study.

Run only the synthetic actor and parser/service fakes in your scratch work. No signed extension, real widget refresh, production account, or course progress is changed by this worked answer. Your submission adds actual results to the ledger and leaves unexecuted checks clearly pending.

simple.story: Two volunteers share a noticeboard but keep separate notebooks. A visitor asks Jo to mark card alpha as read. Jo writes down request r1 and marks it once. The same request arrives again, so Jo leaves the board alone. Then a new club takes over and clears the board. A delayed request from the old club arrives. Jo rejects it because it belongs to the previous club. Sharing the board never meant the volunteers automatically shared their notebook entries.
simple.meaning: An app and extension share code or an entitled container, not memory or actor instances. Repeated commands need an operation identity. Late commands need current account ownership. Durable cross-process writes require their own transaction policy.

example.change: Apply r1 twice, resetOwner(), then apply the old r1 again.
example.after: The outcomes are applied, duplicate, then stale. Alpha appears once before reset and the set stays empty afterward. The old command cannot recreate the cleared card.
